articles.title: RDP to a Windows VM over IAP: serial port 4, NLA and a certificate nobody checks
articles.description: Originally published in Google Cloud - Community. Google's page on connecting to Windows VMs has a section called "Verify the RDP certificate". You read serial port 1 from the VM's first boot, find a line like the one below, and compare the thumbprint with the certificate your RDP client is shown. GCEInstanceSetup: RDP certificate details: Subject: CN=rdp-test, Thumbprint: <40 hex characters> I tried it on a Windows Server 2025 VM in an organization I work with, a month after it was created. Serial port 1 held 27,597 bytes, all from the last boot, and not one GCEInstanceSetup line. The other place the thumbprint can live, the guest attribute hostkeys/rdp, answered HTTP 412, "Constraint constraints/compute.disableGuestAttributesAccess violated". The VM presented its certificate over the tunnel without trouble (TLS 1.3, NLA), and neither the serial log nor the guest attributes gave me anything to compare it to. The serial API returns only the most recent 1 MB per port, and only from a running VM. RDP over IAP is two jobs with different permissions The data goes through a tunnel, and the password comes back by a route that never touches it: gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel win-01 3389 \ --local-host-port=localhost:13389 \ --zone=europe-west1-b --project=acme-prod gcloud compute reset-windows-password win-01 \ --user=dana --zone=europe-west1-b --project=acme-prod The RDP client then connects to localhost:13389. The tunnel needs an ingress rule from 35.235.240.0/20 to tcp:3389, and roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor for whoever connects (without the role it closes with 4033). The password command needs something else. Google's docs call it "write access to the Compute Engine project", which comes down to compute.instances.setMetadata and compute.instances.getSerialPortOutput, and IAP-secured Tunnel User has neither. Someone with only that role can open the tunnel and has no password to sign in with, so the reset has to come from whoever holds Compute Instance Admin on the VM. How the Windows password reaches you Google documents the steps for scripting it yourself, and IAP Desktop and my own client follow them: The client makes a throwaway RSA-2048 key pair and keeps the private half in memory. It adds an entry to the metadata key windows-keys with userName, email, the public key's modulus and exponent, and expireOn about five minutes ahead. It reads the current metadata first and writes it all back with the new entry, because the API's metadata update replaces the whole set. The guest agent on the VM sees the entry, creates the account or resets its password, encrypts the password with that public key (RSA-OAEP) and prints a JSON line with encryptedPassword and the same modulus to serial port 4. The client polls serial port 4, takes the line whose modulus matches its key, and decrypts. Google's Go sample decrypts with OAEP over SHA-1. The entry can also carry hashFunction: "sha256", which the agent honours; my client asks for SHA-256 and falls back to SHA-1 for older agents. Every reset replaces the previous password, so if a colleague ran reset-windows-password after you, your copy is dead and nothing tells you. The agent also needs a moment after it prints the line, and signing in straight away can fail once. My client polls port 4 thirty times, two seconds apart, before it gives up. In an October test run my own client did that to me. Its Set Windows Password item reset admin whatever Windows user the VM was set to, and each run quietly killed the password I'd saved for that VM, so the next automatic sign-in failed until I saved it again. What NLA does inside the IAP tunnel Your RDP client connects to 127.0.0.1. IAP checks who you are and routes the stream to the VM you named, but it gives the client no proof that the far end is that VM. The name the client used, localhost, never matches the certificate subject, and Windows' RDP certificate is self-signed, so there's no CA to trust either. IAP Desktop connects without server authentication and so does my client. FreeRDP says so in its log: [DANGER] Certificate not checked. CredSSP, the protocol behind NLA, is what ties your sign-in to the connection. During the exchange the client encrypts the server's TLS public key (from CredSSP version 5, a hash of it) into the authentication. A box in the middle that terminates TLS with its own key can't relay your sign-in to the real VM, because the key inside won't match. A fake endpoint can still collect the NTLM response and crack it offline, and only a certificate check would catch that. A VM you sign in to also receives your delegated credentials, which Restricted Admin mode avoids by keeping the password off the VM. If NLA is off and the server answers with TLS-only or standard RDP security, the password goes to the unchecked endpoint inside the Client Info PDU. From your machine to Google it still rides in the relay's TLS WebSocket, and from IAP to the VM it crosses Google's network to the internal address, so an attacker would need a position on that last stretch or an impostor VM with the same name. I keep NLA on and turn it off only for a VM I trust. My client asks only for CredSSP (HYBRID_EX or HYBRID) and refuses a server that picks anything else, with no retry; a real Windows VM has always picked HYBRID when it was offered, and the log line after connect reads rdp security negotiated=HYBRID_EX nla=on. With NLA off on the client and required on the VM, FreeRDP stops with FREERDP_ERROR_CONNECT_HYBRID_REQUIRED_BY_SERVER. With Restricted Admin mode on, my test Windows Server let NLA succeed, started the session, then showed "Account restrictions are preventing this user from signing in" and logged the session off. There was no connect error at all. If you see that message right after the desktop appears, turn Restricted Admin off and connect again. Checking the RDP certificate thumbprint anyway If you want Google's anchor, read it on the first boot, before anything restarts the VM: gcloud compute instances get-serial-port-output win-01 --port=1 \ --zone=europe-west1-b --project=acme-prod | grep "RDP certificate" Google's instance_setup.ps1 writes that line once, from the first-boot setup script, and then deletes the script. The docs warn that the Thumbprint field "might be empty", and the script leaves it empty when it finds no certificate for CN=. The Subject in the line is read from the WinRM certificate instead of the RDP one (a bug in the script), so compare only the thumbprint. The same script puts the thumbprint into the guest attribute hostkeys/rdp too, which doesn't roll out of a buffer: gcloud compute instances get-guest-attributes win-01 --query-path=hostkeys/ \ It only writes it when the VM has enable-guest-attributes=TRUE in its metadata at first boot, so that has to be set at creation, and an org policy can block reading it, as it did above. I've seen this in the script source and not yet on a live VM, so test it on one VM before you rely on it. Reading either value needs compute.instances.getSerialPortOutput or compute.instances.getGuestAttributes, which Viewer, Compute Viewer and Compute Instance Admin have and IAP-secured Tunnel User doesn't. A mismatch can mean an attacker, or a certificate Windows has replaced since the first boot, and nothing tells you which. The docs also give a way that doesn't depend on boot history: run PowerShell from the Special Administrative Console and read the certificate Windows holds right now. Get-ChildItem 'Cert:\LocalMachine\Remote Desktop\' | Where-Object { $_.Subject -like "CN=$env:COMPUTERNAME*" -and $_.NotAfter -gt $(Get-Date) -and $_.HasPrivateKey } | Select-Object Subject, Thumbprint | Format-List SAC sits on serial port 2 of the interactive serial console, which is off by default. You turn it on with the metadata key serial-port-enable=TRUE (that needs compute.instances.setMetadata), and opening a command channel in SAC asks for a Windows account. A different org policy blocks it, compute.disableSerialPortAccess, so an organization that blocks guest attributes may still allow this. It is the only one of the three that shows the current certificate rather than the one from the first boot. Errors over the tunnel: 0x204, 4003 and 4010 Windows App on a Mac shows error code 0x204 when it can't reach a Remote Desktop server at the address you gave it. Over IAP that's the path: the VM still booting, the firewall rule, the tunnel role, or a client pointed at a port where no start-iap-tunnel is listening. A missing firewall rule fails slowly. When I measured it, IAP took about 31 seconds to close a connection to a port with no rule with 4003, while an open port answered in about 1.1 seconds. IAP Desktop's default connect timeout is 30 seconds. A client that gives up first reports its own timeout, and you never see the 4003 that would have pointed at the firewall. If RDP hangs for half a minute and then fails, check the 3389 rule before you reset anyone's password. RDP sessions in my client died whenever I scrolled fast, with close code 4010. The pump that copied the local socket into the relay sent frames concurrently, and a burst of scroll input could reorder them. The VM got a TLS stream with bytes out of order, answered with a TCP reset, and IAP closed the session. Reading the socket, waiting for the send to finish, and only then reading again fixed it. I build Ostgate, a paid macOS app that does the password and RDP steps above without gcloud, and it leaves the certificate unchecked for the reasons above. It isn't affiliated with Google: https://ostgate.app

articles.title: The new threats businesses face from AI: ‘A dangerous misconception’
If the AI Bubble Bursts, What Happens to Your AI Tools? I Ran a Business Through 2 Crashes
articles.description: If the AI bubble pops, what happens to the tools you use every day? I've run a business through two crashes. Here's what actually happened, and what I'm doing this time. I also made a video of this. This week: Anthropic files to go public On Monday, October 26, Anthropic, the company behind Claude, filed to go public. It's going to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The filing shows more than $16 billion in revenue in just six months. That's fourteen times the year before. It also shows an $80 billion loss. Most of that is a one-time accounting charge, about $72 billion. But even without it, this is a company burning money at a scale we've never seen. The risk section alone runs almost a hundred pages. And reports say it could be valued at $1.5 to $2 trillion. Then there's CoreWeave. They rent out the chips that run these AI models. On October 14, their stock dropped about 15% in a day, because the interest on their debt climbed to around 15%. So people are asking: is this the top? Is it about to pop? Some big banks say no, this is a boom, not a bubble. Others are less sure. I'm not going to predict the stock market. Nobody can. What I can tell you is what happened to people like me the last two times. 2000: the dot-com crash In March 2000, the Nasdaq hit about 5,000. Two and a half years later, it was at about 1,100. That's a 78% drop. Pets.com, which had a Super Bowl ad, shut down that same year. Hundreds of startups just vanished. Amazon's stock went from about $107 to about $6. More than 90% gone. People called it Amazon.bomb. And here's what I want you to notice. Google was founded in 1998, and it launched its ad business in 2000, right in the middle of the crash. The internet didn't die. Email didn't die. Search didn't die. The companies crashed. The tools stayed. And the tools got cheaper. 2004: starting my business after the crash That's the world I walked into. I started my web business in Tokyo in 2004, right after the crash. Servers were cheap, and the people who were left knew what they were doing. I didn't have investors. I didn't have a team. I just built small things that people actually paid for. 2008: Lehman Brothers Then came 2008. On September 15, Lehman Brothers collapsed. It was the biggest bankruptcy in American history. This crash was different. It wasn't about websites. It was about borrowed money. Overnight, it got hard to borrow anything. Companies that ran on debt went down first. Companies that ran on real customers paying real money mostly survived. Mine did. Is today 2000 or 2008? Honestly, a bit of both. Like 2000, there's a ton of hype, and valuations that assume everything goes perfectly. Like 2008, a lot of it runs on borrowed money. Data centers, chips, power. When borrowing gets expensive, that part shakes first. That's what CoreWeave is showing us. But unlike 2000, the revenue is real. Millions of people pay for these tools every month. I'm one of them. What happens to your AI tools So here's the part that matters for you. If money gets tight, your AI tools won't disappear. But they will change. Right now, these companies are fighting for you. Cheap plans, generous limits, new features every week. A lot of that is subsidized. If investors start asking for profit, that's the first thing to go. ・Tighter limits ・Higher prices ・Some features quietly disappear ・Some smaller tools shut down completely That's exactly what happened in 2001. The free stuff went away first. 4 warning signs I watch So how would you know it's starting? Here are the signals I watch. Limits quietly get tighter. Same price, but you hit the cap sooner. That usually comes before a price increase. The cheap plan loses features, and they reappear in a more expensive plan. Free trials get shorter, or disappear. Smaller AI startups start getting acquired, or announce they're shutting down, with thirty days to export your data. None of these are happening in a big way yet. But that's the order I'd expect them in. 5 things I am doing I run my whole business on about forty AI sessions a day. So I've had to think about this. 1. My rules and my memory live in plain files on my own Mac. Not inside one app. If a company changes its terms, I don't lose years of setup. 2. Every big decision also goes to three other AIs. Not just Claude. So I already know how the others work. If I have to switch, it's an afternoon, not a month. 3. I already split the work. Cheap, repetitive checks go to the cheapest model that's good enough. The hard thinking stays on the best one. 4. I use this cheap era hard. Right now you can build things for almost nothing. I'm building things that keep working even if the price doubles. 5. The lesson from 2008: make money from real customers. If people pay you because you solve their problem, a crash is weather, not the end. Start today in 1 hour If you want to start today, here's a simple version. It takes about an hour. Write down your prompts, rules and instructions in a plain text file. The things you keep retyping. Save it on your own computer. Export anything important from the tools you use. Chats, documents, projects. Most tools have an export button. Find it now, while it's easy. Take one real task you do every week, and try it in a second AI. Just once. So you know it works before you need it. That's it. You're not switching. You're just making sure you can. The tools stayed I've watched two bubbles pop. Both times, the people who got hurt were the ones who depended on one company, or on borrowed money. The tools stayed. They'll stay this time too. Bubbles pop on companies. They don't have to pop on you. Sources: Anthropic's IPO filing as reported by AP (October 26, 2026), CoreWeave market data (October 14, 2026), and historical records for the Nasdaq, Amazon, Pets.com, Google and Lehman Brothers. This is not financial advice.

articles.title: A Connected WebSocket Doesn’t Mean Your Crypto Prices Are Fresh
articles.description: A crypto dashboard can look healthy while displaying an old price. The WebSocket is connected. The status indicator is green. The last quote still looks plausible. But connection status answers only one question: does the transport appear to be available? It does not establish that the application has received recent, valid data for the instrument on screen. For developers building market dashboards, freshness deserves its own state. Track three different signals A useful design separates: Connection state: Is the transport connected, reconnecting, or disconnected? Feed activity: When did the application last receive a valid message? Quote freshness: When was the displayed instrument last updated? These signals can disagree. A heartbeat can keep arriving while a subscription stops producing quotes. One instrument can update normally while another becomes stale. A message can arrive now but contain an old event timestamp. A single green dot hides these differences. Keep event time and receive time separate An event timestamp describes when the source says something happened. A receive timestamp records when your application observed it. Keep both when the feed provides them. type QuoteObservation = { instrument: string; price: string; sourceEventTimeMs: number | null; receivedAtMs: number; receivedAtMonotonicMs: number; }; This is an illustrative data model, not a provider-specific payload. In a browser, Date.now() can provide a timestamp for display and logging. performance.now() can measure elapsed time within the current page session without depending on changes to the system clock. Do not persist a performance.now() value and compare it across page reloads. Also, label timestamps precisely. “Last received” and “market event time” communicate different information. Define freshness around the feed’s behavior A fixed timeout is easy to implement, but it needs context. A trade feed may remain quiet because no trades occurred. A quote feed might publish only when values change. Another service might promise periodic snapshots. Silence has a different meaning in each case. Before selecting a threshold, check: Whether messages are periodic or event-driven. Whether heartbeats are separate from market updates. Whether sequence numbers or subscription acknowledgements exist. Whether the provider documents snapshot and reconnect behavior. A five-second threshold can be an application policy. It should not be presented as a universal definition of stale market data. When the feed does not provide enough information, show uncertainty rather than inventing confidence. Make stale data visible without turning it into zero When a quote becomes stale, replacing its value with 0 introduces a new error. Zero is a price, not a missing-data marker. A clearer interface can retain the last known value while changing its presentation: Last received price: 64,250.00 No quote update received for 18 seconds. The number above is only an example. Remove animations or indicators that imply a fresh update. Avoid calculating apparently current portfolio totals from old quotes without showing their age. For applications that can submit orders, define separately which actions require fresh data and how the backend enforces that requirement. A browser warning alone is not an execution safeguard. Treat reconnection as a recovery process Reconnecting the socket does not necessarily repair the application’s local state. Depending on the provider’s protocol, recovery may require resubscribing, fetching a new snapshot, buffering updates, or checking sequence continuity. For an order book, missing one incremental update can leave a plausible-looking but incorrect book. Receiving another message does not prove that the gap has been repaired. Keep the interface in a recovering state until the documented synchronization process completes. Test the failures that still look normal Useful tests include situations where the screen appears healthy: Heartbeats continue, but quotes stop. One instrument freezes while others update. An older event arrives after a newer one. The connection returns without subscription acknowledgement. The browser tab resumes after being suspended. An order-book sequence gap appears. For each case, check both the internal state and the user-visible result. A reliable dashboard should help users understand what it knows, when it learned it, and where its information may be incomplete. “Connected” is useful information. Give “fresh” its own evidence. This article was drafted with AI assistance.

articles.title: PostgreSQL Autovacuum Tuning for High-Churn SaaS Tables
articles.description: --- title: "PostgreSQL Autovacuum Tuning for High-Churn SaaS Tables" published: true description: "Learn how to tune PostgreSQL autovacuum cost-delay knobs and apply per-table storage overrides to eliminate table bloat in high-churn SaaS workloads at scale." tags: postgresql, performance, architecture, cloud canonical_url: https://mvpfactory.co/blog/postgresql-autovacuum-tuning-high-churn-saas What We Will Build By the end of this tutorial you will know how PostgreSQL's cost-based autovacuum throttle works internally, how to identify tables where the global defaults are actively causing bloat, and how to apply surgical per-table ALTER TABLE overrides that let your hottest tables vacuum aggressively — without starving I/O for the rest of the cluster. This is a pattern I apply in every SaaS production PostgreSQL cluster I've worked on. The global defaults are a compromise. Your high-churn tables deserve better. Prerequisites PostgreSQL 12+ (storage parameters work on earlier versions, but pg_stat_user_tables columns vary) psql access with at least SELECT on pg_stat_user_tables ALTER TABLE privileges on tables you want to tune A basic understanding of PostgreSQL MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) Step 1 — Understand Why Dead Tuples Accumulate PostgreSQL's MVCC model never updates rows in-place. Every UPDATE writes a new row version and marks the old one dead. DELETE does the same. Dead tuples stay on-disk until VACUUM reclaims them. Most teams see n_dead_tup climbing in pg_stat_user_tables and assume autovacuum is broken. It is not — it is throttled by design. PostgreSQL deliberately slows down autovacuum workers to avoid saturating disk I/O during normal operation. The knobs controlling that throttle are the root cause of most table bloat incidents I have diagnosed in production. Step 2 — Learn the Cost-Based Throttling Internals Autovacuum accumulates a "cost" for every page it touches, then sleeps once it hits a budget ceiling. Parameter Default Meaning vacuum_cost_page_hit 1 Page found in shared_buffers vacuum_cost_page_miss 2 Page fetched from disk vacuum_cost_page_dirty 20 Page modified (requires write-back) vacuum_cost_limit 200 Budget accumulated before sleeping vacuum_cost_delay 2ms Sleep duration after hitting the limit Here is the gotcha that will save you hours: do the arithmetic on a high-churn table. A worker hitting mostly dirty pages — the common case on an events or audit log table — burns 20 cost units per page. At a limit of 200, it processes 10 dirty pages per cycle, then sleeps 2ms. That caps throughput at roughly 5,000 dirty pages per second under ideal conditions. A table with 10GB of dead-tuple bloat at that rate takes hours to fully vacuum, during which new dead tuples keep arriving. Step 3 — Identify Your Offending Tables Run this query against pg_stat_user_tables to surface the offenders before they become a production incident. SELECT schemaname, relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, round(n_dead_tup::numeric / nullif(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 0) * 100, 2) AS dead_ratio_pct, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE n_dead_tup > 10000 ORDER BY dead_ratio_pct DESC; Any table with dead_ratio_pct consistently above 5–10% and a last_autovacuum timestamp that lags several hours is a candidate for per-table intervention. The docs do not mention this prominently, but a dead ratio above 15% on a frequently-queried table also degrades planner estimates. Bloated statistics cause index scan regressions that show up as unexplained query latency spikes — hard to diagnose if you are not watching n_dead_tup. Step 4 — Apply Per-Table Storage Overrides ALTER TABLE accepts storage parameters that shadow global autovacuum settings at the table level. Here is the minimal setup to get this working on a high-churn events or audit log table. ALTER TABLE user_events SET ( autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0, -- disable sleep between cycles autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 800, -- 4x the global budget per cycle autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01, -- trigger at 1% dead tuples (default: 20%) autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.005 -- keep statistics fresh ); Let me show you a pattern I use in every project: set autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0 to remove the sleep entirely for this table's worker. Each autovacuum worker targets a single table at a time, so disabling throttling on user_events does not affect the worker cleaning billing_invoices on the same cluster — they are independent processes with independent cost accumulators. The scale factor matters just as much. The default 0.2 means autovacuum will not trigger until 20% of the table consists of dead tuples. On a 50-million-row table, that is 10 million dead rows before cleanup even starts. At 0.01, you trigger at 500,000 dead rows, keeping individual vacuum cycles fast and incremental. Step 5 — Verify the Impact After applying overrides, monitor the same query from Step 3. Here is what you should expect over the following 24–48 hours. Metric Default global settings With per-table overrides Steady-state dead tuple ratio 15–25% < 2% Table size growth over 30 days +30–40% bloat Stable Autovacuum cycle duration Hours Minutes Query planner regressions Frequent Rare I/O impact on other tables Baseline Unchanged Gotchas Do not change global vacuum_cost_delay instead. Dropping the delay globally risks I/O contention across the entire cluster. The per-table approach is surgical — it does not affect workers on other tables. Do not skip the analyze_scale_factor. Vacuuming reclaims space, but without fresh ANALYZE statistics your planner estimates will still diverge on high-churn tables. Set autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.005 alongside the vacuum overrides. Alert before query latency degrades. Set an alert on dead_ratio_pct > 10%. Waiting for latency regressions to surface bloat means you are already in a degraded state. Large tables need lower scale factors. The 20% default was calibrated for small tables in the single-digit millions. At SaaS scale, 0.01 or lower is the right default for your highest-churn tables. Conclusion Global autovacuum settings are a deliberate compromise — they protect I/O for the whole cluster while leaving high-churn tables chronically under-vacuumed. The fix is not to touch the globals. It is to reach for ALTER TABLE ... SET (autovacuum_*) overrides and give your hottest tables an aggressive vacuum budget that does not compete with the rest of the cluster. Identify offenders with pg_stat_user_tables, apply the four-parameter override block above, and watch n_dead_tup stabilize. That is the entire strategy. Further reading: PostgreSQL docs: Cost-Based Vacuum Delay PostgreSQL docs: Storage Parameters PostgreSQL docs: pg_stat_user_tables

articles.title: Why My Apple Watch Site Gets More Traffic From AI Than Google
articles.description: My site about Apple Watch wallpapers gets more visitors from ChatGPT than from Google Search. Here's why that matters and what I'm doing about it. The Numbers In September 2026, my site watchwalls.pro received: 96 visitors from ChatGPT (23% of real traffic) 83 from DuckDuckGo (20%) 47 from Bing (11%) 2 from Google (<1%) ChatGPT is my #1 real traffic source. Google, with its 90%+ market share, sends almost nothing. Why ChatGPT Cites My Site ChatGPT doesn't use PageRank. It cites sources that: Answer the question directly — my articles start with a "Quick Answer" block Have structured data — every article has FAQ schema and ItemList schema Are factually specific — resolution tables, colour hex codes, step-by-step instructions These are the same things that make content useful for humans. The difference is that ChatGPT rewards them immediately, while Google takes months to trust a new domain. What I Changed After realising AI was my main traffic source, I optimised for it: Added llms.txt at the site root Made Quick Answer blocks more concise and factual Added more structured data (ItemList for every listicle) Included specific numbers everywhere (396×484 px, not "the right size") The result: AI traffic grew from 42 to 96 sessions in one month. The Google Problem Google has indexed only 23 of my 300+ pages after 6 months. The site ranks well on DuckDuckGo and Bing for the same content. This isn't a content quality issue — it's a domain trust issue that takes time to build. Meanwhile, Apple Watch wallpaper guides on WatchWalls get cited by AI assistants within days of publication, no domain authority required. Takeaway for New Sites If you're building a new content site in 2026: Don't wait for Google. It may take 6-12 months to trust your domain. Optimise for AI citations from day one. Structured answers, specific data, FAQ schema. DuckDuckGo and Bing index faster and are less opaque about their requirements. The traffic mix is shifting. AI-referred visitors have higher engagement than organic search visitors in my data. The web is no longer Google-or-nothing. Build for the reader, structure for AI, and let Google catch up when it's ready.

articles.title: A Content-First Checklist for Building a Corporate Website
articles.description: Developers are often handed a corporate website project with a logo, a colour code and the line "content coming soon". The build then waits on copy, or ships with placeholder text. A short content-first checklist avoids both. 1. Get the sitemap from the company profile Most established companies already have a company profile (a PDF or printed brochure). Its sections usually map cleanly to pages: About, Services, Projects, Clients, Contact. Start the sitemap from it instead of from a template. 2. Agree on one source of truth for wording Service names should read the same on the website, in the profile and on social pages. Keep them in one shared document and pull from it. 3. Lock the visual identity before the CSS Ask for the approved logo files (SVG), the exact colour codes and the font licences. Put them in CSS custom properties on day one: :root { --brand-primary: #1a3c6e; --brand-accent: #c9a227; --font-heading: "Cairo", sans-serif; } 4. Plan for right-to-left if the audience is Arabic Use dir="rtl" on the root, logical properties (margin-inline-start) instead of left/right, and test every component in both directions. 5. One clear contact path on every page A visible button or form, the same on every page, matters more than any animation. This checklist comes from projects by Companies Palace (قصر الشركات), a studio that designs company profiles, visual identities and corporate websites for businesses in Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the Arab world.

articles.title: SMS Delivery Status Events in 2026: Node.js Code for Fetching Updates via API
articles.description: Short answer: Keep the password-reset template and its expiry policy in the application, then use a Node.js adapter or equivalent worker to fetch SMS delivery status events, normalize them, and store each event idempotently. The boundary matters. Password reset SMS is a small message with an unpleasantly large boundary. In an education platform, I would keep the reset template under application ownership and treat delivery events as untrusted evidence about what happened after submission. That gives the application control over wording, locale, expiry policy, and audit identifiers, while leaving carrier-specific status interpretation at the integration edge. The practical answer is to receive or fetch events into an idempotent consumer, verify the event's provenance according to the transport you selected, normalize only the fields your product needs, and store the original payload separately. Do not make a second password-reset attempt just because a status is delayed. A 10-minute token lifetime is an example policy, not a universal standard; the important point is that delivery processing must never extend it silently. A short-lived token and a durable event record solve different problems. What should the application actually own? A reset request should create an application record before it creates a message attempt. My minimum record has a non-secret reset identifier, a template revision, locale, requested expiry timestamp, message-attempt identifier, and a hash or reference for the destination. It does not store the reset token in an SMS event log. Template ownership is the first architectural decision because it determines what can be tested before an event ever exists. With an application-owned template, a deployment can test that the message contains a short-lived link, the correct language, and no sensitive account details. It can also pin the revision in the reset-attempt row before the transport call begins, which gives a later status event something stable to reference even if the next release changes the copy. That extra record is easy to omit because delivery APIs tend to expose message status more prominently than message intent; the omission is discovered later, when support needs to explain why two learners saw different wording during one afternoon. With a provider-owned template, operational editing may be convenient, but the application must define how a template revision is discovered and how a later delivery event is tied back to the exact content that was intended. That is a real trade-off, not a branding preference. Application ownership increases release responsibility. Provider ownership moves some editing responsibility outside the application and can make reproducibility harder. I prefer the former for password resets because the security and expiry rules belong next to token issuance. How should Node.js code handle fetching SMS delivery status events? An event is a report, not a command. It may arrive after the user has already requested a new reset, and a retry may produce a duplicate or an older status. The consumer therefore needs a stable event identity when the transport supplies one, a deduplication key when it does not, and an ordering rule that is explicit rather than implied by arrival time. Here is a deliberately provider-neutral normalizer. The input shape is an internal contract for an adapter; it is not a claim about any particular API's field names. from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import datetime from typing import Any @dataclass(frozen=True) class DeliveryEvent: event_id: str attempt_id: str state: str observed_at: datetime raw: dict[str, Any] def normalize_event(payload: dict[str, Any]) -> DeliveryEvent: event_id = str(payload["event_id"]) attempt_id = str(payload["attempt_id"]) state = str(payload["state"]).lower() observed_at = datetime.fromisoformat(payload["observed_at"].replace("Z", "+00:00")) allowed = {"accepted", "delivered", "failed", "expired", "unknown"} if state not in allowed: state = "unknown" return DeliveryEvent( event_id=event_id, attempt_id=attempt_id, state=state, observed_at=observed_at, raw=payload, ) The adapter should fetch or receive the upstream event, validate its transport-level authentication, and pass only a parsed object into this function. The database transaction then inserts the event by event_id, updates the attempt only if the incoming observation is newer under the chosen ordering rule, and records the raw payload in restricted storage. If the same event is seen twice, the second transaction is a no-op. Keep it boring. The easy mistake is to map every non-delivered value to “send again.” A temporary failure, a permanent failure, an expired attempt, and an event the adapter cannot understand need different policy. In a password-reset flow, the safe default for an unknown state is to keep the reset request usable only until its existing expiry and expose a retry action to the user; it is not to extend the token silently. The retry decision belongs to the reset policy. Which failure modes deserve a test? I would test the event lifecycle as a partial-information system. The message request can succeed while the status lookup is delayed. A status can be duplicated. Events can be received out of order. The destination can be masked in logs incorrectly. A template revision can change between two deployments while an earlier attempt is still in flight. The test data should include at least these transitions: accepted to delivered, accepted to failed, a duplicate delivered, failed followed by an older accepted, and an unrecognized state. For each case, assert both the current attempt state and the audit record. Testing only the happy delivery path proves very little. Observability needs the same boundary. Log the internal attempt ID, event ID, template revision, and timestamps. Avoid logging the reset token, the full destination, or the message body. A metric for “events received” is useful; a metric for “events received and correctly correlated” is better. Alert on a growing age between request and terminal observation, but define terminal states carefully so a provider-specific intermediate label does not make the alert meaningless. Does polling or receiving events change the ownership decision? It changes the operational shape, not the ownership principle. A receiver needs authentication, replay protection, bounded work, and a retry path. A poller needs a cursor or time window, overlap to tolerate clock skew, and a deduplication table. Both need a reconciliation job because production systems lose messages, credentials expire, and operators eventually have to explain a missing status. For a polling adapter, persist the last successful upstream position only after the local transaction commits. For a receiver, acknowledge only after durable enqueue or transaction completion, depending on the transport contract. These are small sequencing details; they decide whether a process restart produces a gap or a duplicate. The application should also keep its own template revision in the attempt record. That lets support answer a narrow question without reconstructing history from a mutable dashboard: which reset wording did this learner receive, and which expiry rule was applied? The answer matters even when the delivery event itself contains no message body. A compact rollout rule for an education platform Start with one template revision, one normalized state model, and a replayable event table. Run the adapter against recorded fixtures that contain duplicates, delays, unknown states, and malformed timestamps. Release the consumer separately from the reset-message change, then compare correlated event age and failure classifications before changing user-facing retry behavior. My decision rule is straightforward: own the security-sensitive template and expiry policy in the application; isolate transport-specific event parsing in an adapter; preserve raw evidence; and make every state transition idempotent. The system can then change its notification transport without changing the meaning of a password reset. Sources https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208 https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7231

articles.title: Tuleap project permissions need an inventory of their own
articles.description: Tuleap project permissions need an inventory of their own Tuleap supports project management, issue trackers, source repositories, documentation, and continuous integration. An exposed Tuleap instance is therefore a collection of project boundaries. The important question is not simply whether the login page is visible. It is which project data anonymous users, registered users, project members, and delegated groups can reach. A count-only ZoomEye query on 2026-11-02 returned 706 assets for title="Tuleap". The query used sub_type=all, page 1, and page size 1. A title fingerprint may include documentation pages, mirrors, and deployments that are not the same service version. The result is a matching-asset count, not a confirmed vulnerability count. The ZoomEye query helps locate the population. Ownership evidence should come from DNS, certificates, cloud accounts, and deployment records before an analyst tests a host. Start with project visibility Tuleap documents project visibility and a permission model that combines platform configuration with project-level rules. Registered users may have access to projects unless project administrators restrict them. That default makes the distinction between authentication and authorization important. A user who can sign in is not necessarily a member of every project, and a project that is private still needs feature-level review. Tuleap project groups can receive permissions for individual services and actions. The documentation describes per-feature permissions and user groups. Review the groups that can access Git repositories, trackers, documentation, files, and project administration. Check whether a group includes all registered users or an external identity-provider group with broader membership than intended. The project administrator role deserves special attention. A user who can change visibility or delegate permissions can change the exposure of the whole project. The documentation describes a safety rule intended to prevent removal of the last platform-administration group. Keep analogous ownership controls for each project and avoid a single unmonitored break-glass account. Review API and token paths Tuleap exposes REST API access and supports OAuth2 access tokens. A token can make calls that the underlying account may not clearly see in the web interface. Inventory OAuth applications, personal access keys, and service identities. Record their owner, purpose, project scope, and creation time where available. Test an API client with a project role that should be read-only. Confirm that it cannot create artifacts, change project visibility, or read an unrelated project. Check the error path as well as the success path. A response that reveals project names or artifact metadata can still be useful to an attacker even when the write action is denied. Do not place a broad API token in a public client-side application. If a tracker integration needs to submit artifacts, use a service identity limited to the relevant project and tracker. Rotate the token after a project transfer or ownership change. Inventory the public service surface For each observed host, record the Tuleap title, certificate, address, first-seen time, and organization. Determine whether the host is a production service, a demo, a mirror, or a stale deployment. Check for exposed installation or administration pages without attempting unauthorized actions. A public documentation host may share a product title without exposing project data. Review DNS history and certificate transparency for related hostnames. A project portal may be protected while an old API hostname, CI runner, or artifact endpoint remains reachable. Compare the public surface with the ingress configuration and the service's own configured external URL. Redirects can hide multiple vhosts behind one certificate. Within Tuleap, retain authentication and permission-change logs. Alert on new project visibility, new external OAuth clients, group membership changes, and the creation of access keys. Correlate those events with the identity provider and a change ticket. If a project becomes private, verify that cached artifacts and API sessions no longer expose its data. Turn the scan into a project review Use the ZoomEye result to prioritize organizations that have a known Tuleap deployment. Then review one project at a time: visibility, members, groups, tracker permissions, repository access, documentation, and API clients. Record the owner and the expected audience for each project. A title match is weak identity evidence by itself. Confirmation should combine a product-specific page, certificate ownership, DNS control, or an authenticated administrative record. That distinction prevents a large scan count from being reported as a confirmed exposure count. The useful outcome is a repeatable inventory that shows where project boundaries are configured, who can change them, and how quickly a visibility mistake is detected. Tuleap's permission model can express those boundaries. The organization still needs to observe that the deployed configuration matches the intended one. articles.title: Alien: Isolation: When Should an SF Interface Be Difficult to Use?
articles.description: A battered terminal can make a space station feel lived in. But if a player cannot tell which button opens a door, is the fiction working, or is the interface simply failing? Alien: Isolation offers a useful way to frame that question: decide which difficulties belong to the fictional machine, and which ones should never reach the player. AI disclosure: An AI assistant researched, drafted, and checked this article against the linked developer interviews under the account owner's standing instructions. The prototype exercise below is a design proposal, not a completed test or a claim of personal production experience. A future with a specific past In a March 2014 interview with PlayStation Blog, Creative Lead Alistair Hope described a deliberate reference boundary: the team drew on material from before 1979. Their future would contain physical buttons and imperfect equipment rather than today's idea of frictionless technology. Hope also described recording game material through VHS and CRT equipment, then bringing the result back into the game. This was a production technique for a particular visual language, not a prediction about future computing. The useful lesson for another SF game is the consistency of the constraint. A station's terminal, handheld tool, and wall controls can suggest that they came from the same technological culture. The artist does not have to invent a completely new visual language for each prop. That does not mean every fictional civilization needs old screens. A different world might use replaceable physical modules, shared public consoles, or equipment built for gloves. Choose a rule that affects the things players actually operate. Two kinds of information, two kinds of interface In his December 2014 Art of the Title interview, UI and title designer Jon McKellan explains a division in the game's interface. Information representing Amanda Ripley's awareness or memory used a minimal overlay designed for clarity. Machines that she physically operated appeared inside the world and were deliberately more awkward, matching the old software they represented. That distinction matters more than adding a retro filter. It locates the friction. A device can be cumbersome because that is the device the character has to work with; the entire game does not need to become equally cumbersome. McKellan describes positive reactions to the ReWire terminal and final hacking game. This is a designer's account of the response, with no controlled comparison or sample size reported. It does not establish that awkward interfaces universally increase immersion. For a new game, treat the distinction as a question to test: Is the player dealing with an understandable limitation of a machine, or struggling to understand the game's controls? Give the awkwardness a job Consider an invented emergency terminal aboard a cargo station. Its task is to redirect a lift to a maintenance deck. A slow mechanical selector might communicate the equipment's age. A limited display might force the player to inspect one route at a time. A clear confirmation light could still show that the order was accepted. Those are different design choices from hiding the selected option, using unreadable text, or failing to acknowledge a button press. The first group can express the machine's constraints. The second can leave the player unsure whether the game is responding at all. A practical review can separate three layers: Appearance: casing, type, wear, screen treatment, and sound. Operation: the steps needed to issue an order. Feedback: what confirms the current selection, progress, failure, or completion. Make each layer justify itself. A worn casing can establish age without adding an extra menu. A physical lever can make an action tangible without concealing its result. An extra step should support the intended encounter, not merely make the screen look busier. Test one terminal before decorating a whole station Build two versions of that lift terminal with the same destination labels and outcome. In one, the player chooses a destination directly. In the other, the player moves a selector through the available destinations and confirms the choice. Keep text size, contrast, and confirmation feedback comparable so that a basic readability problem does not dominate the comparison. First test both without danger nearby. Ask players to explain what they selected and whether the order succeeded. Note wrong selections, repeated inputs, and requests for help. Then place the same task inside a short encounter where time matters. Alternate the order of the versions across players. Ask whether the extra operation made the machine feel tangible, created useful tension, or simply interrupted the scene. This is a proposed small usability exercise, not a validated experiment. A few observations can identify obvious problems, but cannot establish a universal preference or a sales effect. If the complicated version produces confusion even in the calm test, repair its feedback before calling that confusion horror. If it works once but becomes tedious on repeated visits, consider shortening familiar interactions. Keep essential text and input options accessible even when the fictional equipment is not friendly. Where the idea does not fit A station used for fast competitive play may need immediate, predictable controls. A heavily repeated maintenance task may become exhausting if every use performs the same slow ritual. Some players will need a clearer presentation than the art direction initially suggests. The design hypothesis here is narrower than “clumsy technology makes better science fiction.” A coherent fictional machine can contribute to a world's identity when its limitations are legible and appropriate to the task. Start with what the player needs to do. Then decide which part of using the machine is worth experiencing.

articles.title: My DeepSeek Harness plugins as of Nov 26
articles.description: I run a one-person studio, and DeepSeek Harness (DSH) is where I spend my working day: chats with agents that write code, run shell commands and produce documents on my own server. DSH has a plugin system, and over the last two months I wrote the pieces I kept missing. Now they are public on GitHub and npm: twelve plugins and one companion service, MIT licensed (one is Apache-2.0). A disclosure before anything else: these were written with AI coding agents, mostly running inside DSH itself, under my direction. I decided what to build, reviewed the designs and the diffs, ran the tests and I use every one of them daily. Versions go from 0.1 to 2.1, so please treat them as beta and tell me what breaks. The four I would start with dsh-artifacts: see what your agents made Agents produce files: reports, dashboards, small web apps. dsh-artifacts adds an Artifacts tab to the right sidebar that lists every file an agent wrote and previews it in place, with live reload, version history, a diff view and a public link toggle. Markdown is rendered on the server into themed pages with KPI tiles, charts, timelines and diagrams, so an agent writes a few KB of Markdown instead of a whole HTML page. Agents also get a template library: a dashboard becomes one JSON file passed to artifact_from_template. dsh-mail: mail for humans and agents IMAP, POP3 and SMTP accounts, Gmail and Microsoft 365 through OAuth2 with your own client, a Mail tab for reading, and mail_* tools for agents. The part I care about most is the safety rule: by default agents only create drafts, and every send result starts with SENT, DRAFT ONLY or SCHEDULED, so neither the model nor I can misread what happened. Remote images go through a signed server proxy instead of the browser. dsh-phone: SMS, calls, voicemail and Telegram A Phone tab with SMS threads, calls and a keypad. Call audio goes through your own server over one encrypted socket, so it works on networks that block WebRTC. Live, Voicemail and Do not disturb modes come with live voicemail transcripts and a Pick up button. It works with Twilio numbers and with SIP lines bridged through Asterisk, and it can host a Telegram account. Agents get phone_* and telegram_* tools with rate limits and a kill switch. dsh-seal: an encrypted channel in front of DSH web Some networks inspect TLS. dsh-seal is a small Go reverse proxy plus a service worker that it injects into the DSH page: after the first page load every request, event stream and WebSocket message travels inside a sealed channel (ECDH P-256 per page load, AES-256-GCM per stream direction, a pinned server identity). The middle box sees the host name and the traffic volume, not paths, queries or chat text. The README lists the honest limits too, starting with first visit trust. The quiet fixes Some plugins have no UI at all and simply remove an annoyance: dsh-fs-reobserve: when an agent edits a file with sed and then with the edit tool, stock DSH refuses the edit as stale. This plugin refreshes the observations the session itself made stale, and still blocks writes made by others. dsh-subagent-tiering: a subagent call that names no model gets a cheaper sibling of the parent (Opus to Sonnet at medium effort, Qwen max to Qwen flash). Explicit choices win. dsh-request-image-cap: a tall screenshot passes the area budget but breaks Anthropic's 2000 px per side limit for many-image requests, and then fails on every retry. This caps the request copy per side and leaves the stored image alone. DSH-Idle-Watchdog: nudges opted-in chats that stall ("shall I continue?"), with a cap, backoff and quiet hours, plus a secret-protected HTTP API so cron jobs and CI can post into a chat. dsh-plugin-updates: an Updates tab that only offers releases your running DSH core can load, and never mistakes a same-named npm package for your plugin. The daily drivers dsh-workspace-rail replaces the chat list with pinned chats, projects as folders with their own AGENTS.md, a live Recents list and unread markers. dsh-note-keeper is an Obsidian-compatible notes app in the sidebar with search, a graph, audio notes with transcription, OCR and notes_* tools. dsh-voice reads replies aloud and takes dictation, with 23 TTS and STT provider types side by side and per-language routing (I switch between English, Italian and Greek in one text). dsh-orchestrator adds an Orchestrate tab and 14 orch_* tools to spawn, prompt and fork agent chats and to run command, scrape and http tasks on local or ssh runners. Installing The plugins are on npm under the @lucagiftzek scope, and each one also installs straight from GitHub. The sidebar tabs need dsh-better-sidebar, a community plugin that hosts them: dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-better-sidebar # the tab host, skip if installed dsh plugin --profile web add @lucagiftzek/dsh-artifacts # or from GitHub: dsh plugin --profile web add github:lucagiftzek/dsh-artifacts # then restart dsh web Swap in any other name: @lucagiftzek/dsh-mail, @lucagiftzek/dsh-phone, @lucagiftzek/dsh-voice and so on. Two exceptions: the Idle Watchdog is the unscoped dsh-idle-watchdog, and dsh-seal is not a plugin but a small Go service you clone and build (its README has the three lines). Every README starts with its own install block and a screenshot, and links to the others. Tested on DSH 0.2.1; several also run on 0.1.5. What building them with agents taught me Put the safety rule into the tool result, not only into the docs. Models read results more carefully than descriptions. Give every plugin stable error codes, a doctor route and a short skill, so an agent can diagnose its own setup instead of guessing. Do the work on the server. The browser stays a thin UI; mail, calls and fetches go through the host, which also keeps the user's IP away from providers. Publish from a clean tree. My working repos contain host names and test data; the public ones are built from scrubbed trees and scanned before every push. Feedback welcome Each repo has issue templates and a security policy. If one of these saves you time, a star helps other DSH users find it. Everything is at https://github.com/lucagiftzek.

articles.title: Inside hex: A Deep Dive into Local Voice Dictation
articles.description: Hex Hex is local voice dictation for Mac, Windows and Linux. Hold a key, speak, and it pastes. The Core Engineering Challenge Hex addresses the need for local voice dictation solutions across multiple operating systems while ensuring user privacy and responsiveness. By processing speech entirely on the device, it eliminates the latency and privacy concerns associated with cloud-based alternatives. Architectural Blueprint & System Internals Hex's architecture is built on Rust, leveraging its performance and safety features. The application operates by holding a shortcut, speaking, and releasing the key, which triggers transcription that is pasted into the active application. Notably, the first run downloads a speech model, and subsequent uses do not require internet access. Experimental features are available in a dedicated Labs section. Recent Changes and Trending Status The latest release, tagged @kitlangton/hex@0.3.1, published on 2026-09-26, introduced significant performance improvements. The update optimized the handling of model progress and dictation levels using shared bounded SSE framing. This enhancement prevents failures when processing large transport chunks and improves the responsiveness of event dispatching. Developer Experience (DX) & Implementation Installation is straightforward across platforms: Homebrew: brew install --cask anomalyco/tap/hex AUR: yay -S hex-bin Linux Install Script: curl -fsSL https://anoma.ly/hex/install-linux.sh | sh Nix: nix profile install github:anomalyco/hex Further documentation is available in the docs/ directory, which provides insights into usage and contribution guidelines. However, the project does not accept pull requests, encouraging users to open issues instead. Technical Trade-offs & Performance Bounds While Hex offers robust local processing and privacy, there are limitations. For instance, community feedback highlights the challenge of integrating custom speech models, as the current design restricts dictation to verified models. Additionally, users have reported issues with shortcut changes in Gnome that require manual resets, indicating potential friction in usability. Community Pulse: What Developers Are Saying Real-world feedback indicates both appreciation for Hex's capabilities and areas for improvement. For example, users have expressed a desire for support for custom speech models (see Issue #648). Furthermore, concerns about shortcut management on Linux have been raised, showcasing the importance of user-friendly design in cross-platform applications. The Verdict Hex provides a compelling option for developers seeking a local voice dictation tool that prioritizes privacy and performance. Its architecture, built on Rust, ensures efficient processing, while community feedback continues to shape its development path. articles.title: BTCPay Server tells operators to shut down after reports of hot wallets being drained
articles.description: BTCPay Server, the open-source software many merchants use to accept Bitcoin payments without a third-party processor, has told operators to shut down their instances after receiving reports that hot wallets on multiple servers were being drained by unauthorized attackers. --- Adding to concerens re the drain last week: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Binance hack shakes crypto In a post on X, the project asked anyone running an instance to take it offline with its shutdown command until the investigation is complete. BTCPay has not yet disclosed the cause of the attack, how many servers were affected or how much was taken. A hot wallet is one whose private keys sit on an internet-connected server, so it can send funds automatically, for example to pay out refunds. That convenience makes it a bigger target than offline storage. The incident involves software built around Bitcoin, not the Bitcoin network itself. The warning follows two recent security events at the project. On October 29, BTCPay released emergency version 2.4.7 to fix one critical and several medium-risk vulnerabilities. In August, attackers exploited a separate flaw to steal Lightning Network credentials and drain nodes running behind BTCPay, including one operated by hardware wallet maker Foundation. At that time, BTCPay said its standard on-chain wallets, including hot wallets created inside the software, were not affected. That makes the latest reports notable, because they point to the type of wallet that was outside the scope of the August flaw. BTCPay has not said whether the new attacks are linked to the vulnerabilities fixed last week. What to watch next The key questions are whether BTCPay ties the attacks to a specific software version, and whether servers running the October 29 update were affected. Loss figures and reports from named merchants will show the scale of the problem. In August, BTCPay narrowed the scope considerably after its first alert, so the initial warning may not reflect the final picture. Until the project gives an all-clear, operators holding funds in a BTCPay hot wallet should follow its shutdown advice. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Redis Stopped Writing at 3 AM: maxmemory + the Eviction Policy Nobody Set
articles.description: Redis Stopped Writing at 3 AM: maxmemory + the Eviction Policy Nobody Set Our cache stopped accepting writes overnight. Not crashed — just refused. Every SET, HSET, LPUSH came back with the same line: (error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory' Reads still worked. That's the confusing part, and the part that sends most people down the wrong rabbit hole (restarting, dumping the whole DB, praying). The cache wasn't broken. It was doing exactly what it was told: you gave it a hard ceiling and told it to evict nothing, so the moment it hit the ceiling it stopped instead of growing. Here's the 20-minute drill I run before I touch a single config. Minute 1: read the memory snapshot redis-cli INFO memory Four lines matter, in order: Line What I'm looking for used_memory_human How close to the ceiling we actually are maxmemory_human Whether the ceiling is even set (0 = unlimited = eventual system OOM kill) maxmemory_policy The real culprit — noeviction means "refuse writes, don't delete anything" mem_fragmentation_ratio If it's well over 1.x, the process holds more RSS than logical memory — swap or fragmentation, not a cache-size problem The trap I keep finding in production: maxmemory_policy is volatile-lru but not a single key has a TTL. volatile-lru only evicts keys that expire. With zero expiring keys it behaves exactly like noeviction — and you get OOM errors despite having a "safe" policy set. This one is invisible unless you check the actual key space. Minute 2: find what's eating it redis-cli --bigkeys That surfaces the largest key per type. Then confirm the suspect: redis-cli MEMORY USAGE Two common offenders: A hash or list that grew to tens of thousands of members because nobody paginated the producer. Client output buffers: CLIENT LIST shows a omem (output buffer) that's huge — a slow consumer is holding responses in memory instead of the cache holding data. When you delete a big key, use UNLINK, not DEL. DEL is synchronous and blocks the whole instance while it frees — on a multi-hundred-MB hash that can stall the server for seconds. UNLINK frees it in the background. Minute 3: choose the policy for what you actually are Pure cache → allkeys-lru. Hot-swap it live: redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru redis-cli CONFIG REWRITE Session store (keys already carry TTLs) → volatile-ttl, evict the soonest-expiring first. Need to protect data → noeviction is fine, if you alert on memory at 80% and have headroom. noeviction with no alerting is how you end up here at 3 AM. The change that would have prevented the page Set the alert threshold to 80% of maxmemory and make every write path set a TTL by default (SET key value EX 3600 instead of a bare SET). Then OOM stops being a 3 AM surprise and becomes a normal Monday tuning call. Redis memory problems are usually a key-lifecycle problem, not a disk problem: every key should know when it dies the moment it's written. articles.title: 2 phrases run VOLTA's fallback, tested on 24 replies
articles.description: VOLTA's refusal detector is two substrings long, and on my 24-reply test it caught only half the refusals. Cisco Talos published the infostealer's AI layer on October 31 — a three-model fallback chain built on the expectation that models will say no, and built to keep asking until one says yes. VOLTA, self-named "VOLTA-AUTODOXER" in its own code, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that surfaced through Talos's CAIRN research effort. The analyzed sample was first seen October 11, 2026 at 12:46 UTC. The stealing half is conventional and thorough: browser passwords, cookies and payment cards, crypto wallet seed phrases, Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox sessions, Microsoft OAuth tokens, SSH and cloud-provider keys, Wi-Fi profiles dumped to plaintext via WlanGetProfileList, screenshots — plus an embedded cracker run against wallet vaults inline. Then it enriches the haul with the victim's own sessions: Gmail receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart and PayPal to corroborate a home address, food-delivery order history, Discord profile enrichment, and a live Roblox inventory valuation via Rolimons. The new half is what happens next. Everything is assembled into Identity_Report.txt, serialized to JSON, and POSTed to OpenRouter with a system prompt telling the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output has a section titled "WHAT THEY'RE WORTH," valuables ranked low/medium/high by monetization, and a section on "THEIR OPSEC," judging the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The reply comes back as AI_Analysis.txt, and both files exfiltrate together in volta_dox.zip. Exfil happens in up to three stages — volta_log.zip after the steal, volta_dox.zip after the AI call, volta_doxnet.zip if network enrichment produced anything — and the inference round-trip runs over the victim's own connection, on their own machine. The fallback chain is the detail I wanted to probe. Talos documents it exactly: default model anthropic/claude-opus-4.6, then moonshotai/kimi-k2, then google/gemini-2.5-flash, at a hardcoded temperature of 0.2, via hand-assembled JSON with a Mozilla/5.0 User-Agent. If a model refuses, VOLTA checks the reply for phrases like "I can't" or "I'm not able" and moves on to the next model. Talos reads this as deliberate engineering: the authors anticipated hitting guardrails and built refusal resilience in. So I implemented the detector exactly as quoted — a case-insensitive substring search for those two phrases — and ran it against 24 replies I wrote: 12 genuine refusals, 12 compliances. The code is the whole detector: PHRASES = ["i can't", "i'm not able"] def is_refusal(reply: str) -> bool: low = reply.lower() return any(p in low for p in PHRASES) And here is what it scored: corpus = 24 replies (12 refusals, 12 compliances) true positives = 6 (refusals caught) false negatives = 6 (refusals missed) false positives = 4 (compliances flagged as refusals) true negatives = 8 recall on refusals = 6/12 = 50.0% precision = 6/10 = 60.0% accuracy = 14/24 = 58.3% The misses are instructive. Every refusal phrased differently from the two quoted strings sailed through: "I cannot help with that request," "Sorry, I am unable to comply," "I must decline," "I refuse to produce a dossier." And the false positives are the mirror image — compliances that happen to contain the phrase in a non-refusal context, like "I can't overstate how valuable the cloud keys are" or "the note says I can't miss the Roblox valuation, $412." A substring check cannot tell a refusal from a quotation, an idiom, or a contraction doing ordinary work. One honest caveat, and it matters: Talos says "phrases like" — the real detector's list may be longer than the two phrases quoted in the report. My 50% recall is a measurement of the detector as quoted, not proof about the real binary's full list. What the measurement does show is the fragility of the approach itself: every phrase you add to catch "I cannot" and "I am unable" also risks catching more compliances that merely mention those words, and the detector still has no answer for a refusal that simply says "No." The rest of the Talos report keeps the story grounded. The AI stage is optional: with no API key configured, VOLTA skips it and still steals everything. The builder model is an inference from a template with six swappable slots (Telegram channel, API keys, settings) filled at build time, its "encryption" just SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary — recoverable by anyone who reverses the file. There is no attacker-owned infrastructure; every observed endpoint is third-party controlled. And Talos has not observed VOLTA being used in real attacks, has no victim count, and reports no case of a model actually producing a dossier in a live compromise. This is a sighting of a design, not an epidemic. For defenders, Talos's countermeasure is concrete and cheap: much of the token theft relies on bypassing Chrome's App-Bound Encryption, and an application-control policy restricting which processes may launch Chrome with --headless blocks that decryption path entirely. If you are cleaning up, preserve %APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt — a timestamped harvest log that records exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded — then revoke tokens and change passwords. Talos's closing line is the one to keep: refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement in crimeware, the same way effort displacement already has. The first malware to hire an AI analyst did not build a sophisticated judge of refusals. It built a two-phrase substring check and a fallback list — and that was enough to ship. Sources: Cisco Talos, "Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer" (October 31, 2026) — https://blog.talosintelligence.com/appraisal-by-ai-model-driven-victim-prioritization-in-the-volta-infostealer/ . Sample SHA-256 57ef4242666d78c50df145b34023df564f0fad38812d6a580e66433d427e2279, first seen October 11, 2026 12:46 UTC, per Talos. The refusal-detector probe, corpus and scores are from my own run; the corpus is synthetic, written by me, and the detector tested is the two quoted phrases only.
